case_studies.title: Litmus: Zero-Label, Code-Driven Metric Specification for Evaluating AI Systems
case_studies.abstract: As agentic LLM systems move from prototypes to deployment across increasingly diverse domains, evaluating them has become both more important and more difficult. The challenge is not only that individual metrics may be unreliable, but that evaluation goals are often left implicit. Without a clear account of what a system is expected to do, how it can fail, and which failures matter, metric choices become difficult to justify, interpret, or validate. We present Litmus, a zero-label system that designs evaluation and monitoring metrics for AI pipelines by eliciting evaluation intent from source
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating AI systems by designing a zero-label system called Litmus, which creates metrics for AI pipelines without requiring labeled data. Litmus helps clarify evaluation goals and identifies potential failures. The result is a more reliable and justifiable way to assess AI system performance.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI pipelines, here is what to do: review your current evaluation metrics, consider using Litmus to design new metrics, and assess how Litmus can improve the reliability of your AI system evaluations. This flags a risk: if your org uses AI systems without clear evaluation goals, check your metrics immediately to ensure they are valid and justifiable. Not directly applicable to non-AI IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty due to the use of 'Litmus' and 'zero-label system'. Relevant to IT as it involves LLMs and evaluation. Value due to potential for designing evaluation and monitoring metrics.

case_studies.title: MuPPET: A Benchmark for Contextual Privacy of LLM Assistants in Multi-Party Conversations
case_studies.abstract: LLM agents are increasingly deployed in multi-party environments, handling sensitive personal data on behalf of individual users, for instance in group chats. When such an agent discloses private information, it reaches every group member at once. This risk is structurally harder to control than in one-to-one settings, as every piece of private information must be appropriate for every recipient in the group. Yet all existing contextual privacy benchmarks consider only single-interlocutor settings, leaving multi-party privacy risks unmeasured. We introduce MuPPET (Multi-Party Privacy Exposure
case_studies.summary: MuPPET is a benchmark that solves the problem of measuring privacy risks in multi-party conversations involving large language model (LLM) assistants, the researchers built a tool to assess these risks, and the result is a better understanding of how to control private information disclosure in group settings. This is relevant to IT engineers managing cloud infrastructure that handles sensitive personal data. The research focuses on improving privacy in group conversations.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that handles group conversations or multi-party interactions, here is what to do: review your current privacy settings, assess the risk of private information disclosure, and consider implementing additional controls to mitigate these risks. This flags a risk: if your org uses LLM assistants in group chats, check your privacy protocols immediately. Not directly applicable to general IT infrastructure work, but relevant to those handling sensitive personal data in cloud environments.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper introduces a benchmark for multi-party conversation privacy, which may not be directly relevant to IT engineers' work. However, it has some IT relevance due to the use of LLM agents. The novelty of the benchmark and its potential application in real-world impact make it a valuable contribution despite low monetisation potential. Since its total score is above 40, set 'low_signal': false.

case_studies.title: Accuracy and Satisfaction in Multi-Turn LLM Dialogues for NFR Assessment
case_studies.abstract: LLM-based dialogue assistants have become mainstream tools for software developers, yet current evaluation benchmarks focus exclusively on functional correctness. This leaves a critical gap in assessing the quality and accuracy of these conversations when handling Non-Functional Requirements (NFRs), which are inherently vague, context-dependent, and involve many parts of a program. Evaluating how well these systems support collaborative reasoning about NFRs requires methods that go beyond single-turn accuracy to capture both the correctness of the system's outputs and the quality of the multi-
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating the quality and accuracy of LLM-based dialogue assistants in handling Non-Functional Requirements. The authors built a method to assess the correctness and quality of these systems in multi-turn conversations. The result provides a way to capture both the accuracy of the system's outputs and the quality of the conversation.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on the development and evaluation of LLM-based dialogue assistants for software developers.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Paper discusses novel approach to evaluating multi-turn LLM dialogues for NFR assessment, which is surprising for IT professionals working with LLMs. However, the focus is on NLP benchmarks and not directly relevant to IT infrastructure or deployment. The approach has potential to be used by IT engineers to evaluate LLMs, but a specific and actionable guide is not provided within the abstract. Novelty and AI maturity scores are high due to the surprising evaluation method used.

case_studies.title: Grading the Grader: Lessons from Evaluating an Agentic Data Analysis System
case_studies.abstract: Agentic data analysis systems produce rich outputs, including code, numerical results, and verbal diagnostics. This makes them more challenging to evaluate than single-turn LLM responses. It is therefore necessary to distinguish genuine disagreement between an agent's output and a ground-truth answer from grading artifacts. We investigate how reliably automated graders assess such a system and what strategies improve grading quality by applying LAMBDA, a multi-agent data-analysis system, on 153 numerical QRData tasks from DSGym. case_studies.summary: This research evaluates the effectiveness of automated grading systems for agentic data analysis, developing a human-AI grading cascade to improve grading quality. It investigates how to distinguish genuine disagreement from grading artifacts. The result is a more reliable method for assessing complex data analysis systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on evaluating data analysis systems rather than managing cloud infrastructure.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty (10) because of the concept of agentic data analysis systems; IT Relevance (20) despite being in an academic setting, it deals with LLM and automated grading; Value (10) because while specific, it is still a very theoretical application. IT engineers/consultants may learn something but this is unlikely to be of immediate benefit.

case_studies.title: GIF: Locally Sound Geometric Information Flow Control for LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Large language models increasingly mediate interactions between sensitive data, untrusted inputs, and privileged actions in agentic systems, creating security and privacy risks. These range from prompt injections that manipulate downstream tool use to leakage of confidential information through model outputs. Recent Information Flow Control (IFC)-based defenses show promise but lack a principled semantic foundation for reasoning about information flow through the model itself. Since any input token may influence any output token in an autoregressive LLM, existing approaches suffer from severe
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of security and privacy risks in large language models by building a new Information Flow Control system called GIF, which helps control the flow of sensitive data. The result shows promise in defending against prompt injections and leakage of confidential information. This research focuses on language models and not directly on cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on securing large language models, but IT teams responsible for integrating such models into their systems should be aware of the potential security risks and consider using similar information flow control measures in the future. If your organization uses large language models, check the security measures in place to protect sensitive data. This research does not require immediate action from cloud infrastructure managers.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: While not extremely surprising, a principled semantic foundation for reasoning about information flow through the model itself is a unique contribution relevant to IT. Relevance: High score for LLM APIs and security risks. Value: Theoretical potential to apply IFC-based defenses, but specific and actionable implementation details are needed (score: 10).

case_studies.title: Sol Video Inference Engine: Agent-Native Full-Stack Acceleration Framework for Efficient Video Generation
case_studies.abstract: Modern video diffusion models achieve higher generation quality through scaling, but this also increases inference cost. Although many acceleration methods have been proposed, a central challenge is that the most effective acceleration strategy is highly instance-specific: a recipe that works well for one combination of model, hardware, and inference configuration often does not transfer to another. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of high inference costs in video generation models by building a full-stack acceleration framework. The result is a more efficient video generation process. This affects IT infrastructure work related to video processing and AI model deployment.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for video processing or AI model deployment, here is what to do: review your current acceleration strategies, consider implementing instance-specific optimization techniques, and assess the potential benefits of a full-stack acceleration framework like Sol Video Inference Engine.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a new framework for efficient video generation, but its novelty and relevance to IT infrastructure are low. However, it shows some signs of IT relevance due to the use of agent-native technology. The value 90 days is low because it's an academic innovation rather than a practical use case.
